definition: Computational lexicology is a branch of computational linguistics, which is concerned with the use of computers in the study of lexicon.
details: It has been more narrowly described by some scholars (Amsler, 1980) as the use of computers in the study of machine-readable dictionaries. It is distinguished from computational lexicography, which more properly would be the use of computers in the construction of dictionaries, though some researchers have used computational lexicography as synonymous.

explainer.lead: Computational lexicology uses computers to study lexicons: the words and related information collected in a language. It matters because machine-readable dictionaries let researchers examine lexical information computationally rather than only by hand.

tiers.eli5: Think of a dictionary as a giant collection of word cards. Computational lexicology means using a computer to study those cards and learn about the words in them. It is about studying dictionaries, not necessarily writing new ones.
tiers.practitioner: The work centers on computational analysis of lexicons, often using machine-readable dictionaries as the material under study. Keep the goal distinct from computational lexicography, which concerns building dictionaries, while allowing for the fact that some researchers use the terms synonymously.
tiers.paperLevel: Computational lexicology is the branch of computational linguistics concerned with computer use in the study of lexicon. Amsler (1980) described it more narrowly as the use of computers in the study of machine-readable dictionaries; terminology is not fully settled because computational lexicography has sometimes been used as a synonym.

explainer.example: A researcher could use a computer to examine the word entries in a machine-readable dictionary and study how its lexicon is organized.

usedIn.name: Computational linguistics
usedIn.detail: The broader field in which computers are used to study lexicons.

usedIn.name: Machine-readable dictionary research
usedIn.detail: A narrower setting in which dictionary entries are studied with computers.

explainer.intuition: A lexicon contains information about words, and a computer can help researchers study that information. The focus is analysis of lexical material, especially when it is available in machine-readable dictionary form.
howItWorks: Choose a lexicon or machine-readable dictionary to study.
Use a computer to examine its lexical information.
Analyze the results to learn about the lexicon.
explainer.whyItMatters: It gives lexicon research a computational approach and makes machine-readable dictionaries objects of systematic study. It also separates the study of dictionaries from the distinct task of using computers to construct them.
misconceptions: It is not necessarily the computer-assisted construction of dictionaries; that is more properly computational lexicography.
The boundary is not universally observed, because some researchers use computational lexicography as a synonym.
Its scope can be broad lexicon study or, more narrowly, the study of machine-readable dictionaries.
